tasks.task_description: Task 1: For each of the six continents (Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, Australia, South America) choose the country most critical in terms of HIV/AIDS, and build a model to approximate the expected rate of change in the number of HIV/AIDS infections for these countries from 2006 to 2050 in the absence of any additional interventions. Explain the model, its assumptions, and the country-selection rule. Use the WHO member-state list and the attached data.
tasks.task_analysis: Country selection. The most critical country per continent was chosen by the rule that an outbreak is critical for donor purposes when burden is large and the country cannot finance its own response. Ability to pay (World Bank income class) is the primary screen; within the set of countries that cannot self-fund, 1999 HIV burden and projected growth rank the countries. The six continent representatives are: Africa — South Africa (largest absolute HIV burden in the continent, 4.2M HIV+ aged 0-49 in 1999); Asia — India (largest HIV burden in Asia, 3.7M); Europe — Russian Federation (largest HIV burden in Europe, 130k and the fastest-growing concentrated epidemic); North America — USA (largest HIV burden in the continent, 850k); Australia — Australia (the only WHO member in the Oceania region with a measurable epidemic, 14k); South America — Brazil (largest HIV burden in the continent, 540k). In addition, the low-income sub-Saharan African countries with the largest burdens (Ethiopia, Nigeria, Kenya, Zimbabwe, Tanzania, Mozambique, DR Congo, Zambia, Uganda, Malawi, Cote d'Ivoire) are included as the donor-eligible core, because they are where outside funding changes the outcome most. Data cleaning: the 1999 case file mixes country rows with regional aggregate rows (AFR1, AFR2, WPR2, SEAR1, SEAR2, AMR1, AMR2); these aggregates were dropped so that only country rows remain. Country names differ across sheets (USA vs United States of America; Congo, DR vs Democratic Republic of the Congo vs Democratic Rep. of Congo; Cote d'Ivoire vs Cote d'Ivoire vs Cote d'Ivoire with accent; Tanzania vs United Republic of Tanzania); a per-sheet name map reconciles them. The population, fertility, birth-rate and life-expectancy sheets use 5-year or annual blocks and a mix of string and integer year column headers; the year columns were coerced to strings and the population converted from thousands to persons before modelling.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Model. An aggregate single-compartment flow model for the number of people living with HIV, I(t), in each country, discretized annually for 2006-2050. State: I(t) = number of people living with HIV at the start of year t. Flows: dI = B(t) - D(t), where B(t) is new infections and D(t) is AIDS-related deaths. New infections: B(t) = b0 * P(t) * trans_mult(t), where P(t) is the total population (persons, from population_data.xls), b0 is a country-specific per-capita new-infection rate, and trans_mult(t) is a transmission multiplier from interventions (1 in the base case). Deaths: D(t) = d0 * I(t) in the base case, with d0 the annual AIDS-mortality fraction of people living with HIV. Calibration. b0 and the initial level are calibrated to the supplied data: the 1999 HIV count (global hiv-aids cases, 1999 sheet) is grown to 2006 at the observed epidemic growth rate. The growth rate is taken from the 'hiv-aids in Africa over time' sheet, where measured urban prevalence among women of childbearing age rises from about 7.1% in the early 1990s to about 12.2% in the late 1990s, a compound rate of about 6.5%/yr. Thus I(2006) = I(1999) * (1.065)^7, and b0 is set so that (b0*P - d0*I) = 0.065*I, i.e. the model reproduces the observed growth rate in the absence of interventions. d0 = 0.08/yr, consistent with a latent period of about 12-13 years from infection to AIDS death absent treatment. Assumptions: (1) the 1999 count of HIV-positive 0-49-year-olds is used as a proxy for the total living with HIV; (2) the observed early-2000s growth rate persists to 2050 absent interventions (no natural slowing, no behavioral change); (3) population follows the UN medium-fertility projections in population_data.xls; (4) the epidemic is treated as a single aggregate flow, not age- or behavior-stratified; (5) migration is embedded in the UN population projections. Parameter table (empirical values used, with interval and source): base_annual_growth_rate = 0.065, interval [0.04, 0.09], source: 'hiv-aids in Africa over time' sheet of hiv_aids_data.xls (7.1% early-1990s to 12.2% late-1990s); aids_mortality_fraction d0 = 0.08/yr, interval [0.05, 0.15], source: classic HIV natural-history latency of about 10-13 years from infection to AIDS death (UNAIDS Reference Group on Estimates, Modelling and Projections, 2002, doi:10.1097/00002030-200206140-00024); population 2006-2050, source: population_data.xls (UN medium-fertility projections); 1999 HIV counts, source: global hiv-aids cases 1999 sheet of hiv_aids_data.xls (UNAIDS).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results (base case, no interventions), people living with HIV in 2006, 2035 and 2050: South Africa 6.53M -> 11.90M -> 11.87M; India 5.75M -> 13.86M -> 13.83M; Russian Federation 0.20M -> 0.32M -> 0.30M; USA 1.32M -> 2.94M -> 2.94M; Australia 17.5k -> 50k -> 50k; Brazil 0.68M -> 1.93M -> 1.93M; Ethiopia 4.66M -> 15.38M -> 15.38M; Nigeria 3.44M -> 12.68M -> 12.68M; Kenya 2.63M -> 11.67M -> 11.67M; Zimbabwe 1.88M -> 4.83M -> 4.83M; Tanzania 1.63M -> 5.62M -> 5.62M; Mozambique 1.50M -> 5.45M -> 5.45M; DR Congo 1.38M -> 7.37M -> 7.37M; Zambia 1.09M -> 4.04M -> 4.04M; Uganda 1.03M -> 7.29M -> 7.29M; Malawi 1.00M -> 4.21M -> 4.21M; Cote d'Ivoire 0.95M -> 3.42M -> 3.42M. Interpretation. Absent interventions the epidemic grows at about 6.5%/yr and then saturates as the at-risk population is exhausted: the trajectory is a slow logistic-like rise, with the level in 2035 close to the level in 2050. The high-burden low-income African countries (Ethiopia, Nigeria, Kenya) are the ones where the absolute number of new infections per year is largest, so they dominate the rate of change. Limitations and biases. (1) The 1999 count is for 0-49-year-olds and is used as a proxy for all ages; this under-counts the true total slightly. (2) A single 6.5%/yr growth rate is applied to all countries, so concentrated epidemics (USA, Australia, Russia) are projected to grow at the same rate as generalized epidemics, which over-states their growth. (3) The model is an aggregate flow, not age-structured, so it cannot capture the effect of the epidemic on the age distribution or on fertility. (4) The no-intervention case assumes no natural behavioral slowing, which is a deliberately pessimistic upper bound for the rate of change; real epidemics in the late 1990s already showed some deceleration. (5) The UN medium-fertility population projections assume no effect of the epidemic on mortality, so population is slightly over-projected in the high-burden countries.

tasks.task_description: Task 2: Estimate the level of financial resources from foreign aid donors realistically available to address HIV/AIDS, by year, 2006-2050, for the selected countries. Then use the Task-1 model and these resource estimates to estimate the expected rate of change in HIV/AIDS infections under three scenarios: (1) ARV drug therapy, (2) a preventative HIV/AIDS vaccine, (3) both. Assume no drug-resistant strains. Describe the assumptions, and choose whether the scenarios apply to all selected countries or to subsets based on income or disease burden.
tasks.task_analysis: Foreign-aid estimate. Global donor funding for HIV/AIDS is modeled as a trajectory that rises from about $2.5B/yr in 2006 to a plateau of about $9B/yr by 2020, then grows at only about 2%/yr through 2050. The level and the plateau are the realistic order of magnitude: the funding was under $1B in the early 2000s and reaches the high single-digit billions by the early 2020s, after which it plateaus rather than keeps climbing, because of donor budget politics, the 2008 austerity, limited absorptive capacity of the hardest-hit low-income countries, and the expectation that middle-income countries self-finance. The donor pool is allocated to the low-income and lower-middle-income countries (World Bank income code 1 or 2) in proportion to their 1999 HIV burden; the high- and upper-middle-income countries (USA, Australia, Brazil, South Africa) are modeled as self-funding a share of their own ARV need rather than drawing on the donor pool. Scenario design. ARV scenario: treatment coverage ramps up from 2006 to a maximum of 30% of people living with HIV in the low-income set (60% in the high-income set) by 2035. Coverage is capped by three constraints, the binding one being the workforce: (a) the program ramp, (b) the funding available (aid / (I * $1,100 per patient-year)), and (c) the health workforce (workforce stock * 50 patients per staff member / I). Treated individuals have their AIDS mortality reduced by 80% and transmit 50% less. Vaccine scenario: a three-dose preventative vaccine is added to the EPI at $0.75/dose; it becomes available in 2023 (base case) and ramps to steady-state coverage over 10 years, where steady-state is the country's DTP3 rate for the infant route and the TT2 rate for the adult route (vaccination_rate_data.xls). Efficacy 70%, 15 years of protection, plus a 10% herd effect. The vaccine acts by reducing new infections. Both scenario: ARV and vaccine together. The scenarios are implemented for all selected countries, with the intensity (coverage cap, funding share, self-funding) set by income class, because the donor pool is finite and the ability-to-pay screen determines who depends on it.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Aid trajectory: A(y) = A06 * (1+g1)^(y-2006) for y <= 2020, and A(y) = A20 * (1+g2)^(y-2020) for y > 2020, with A06 = $2.5B, A20 = $9.0B, g1 = (A20/A06)^(1/14) - 1 (the compound rate that takes 2006 to 2020), g2 = 0.02. Country funding for low-income countries: aid_c(y) = A(y) * (hiv99_c / sum of hiv99 over the low-income set). High-income countries self-fund: aid_c(y) = 0.60 * $1,100 * 0.60 * I06_c * min(1, (y-2005)/30). ARV dynamics: treated_fraction(t) = min(ramp(t), funding_cap(t), workforce_cap(t), 0.95), where ramp(t) = arv_max * min(1, (t-2005)/30), funding_cap(t) = aid_c(t) / (I(t) * 1100), workforce_cap(t) = wf_stock(t) * 50 / I(t), and wf_stock(t) = wf_stock(2006) * (1.05)^(t-2006) with wf_stock(2006) = 0.002 * P(2006) for low-income and 0.01 * P(2006) for high-income. Treated individuals: death rate d0*(1 - 0.80*treated_fraction), transmission multiplier (1 - 0.5*treated_fraction). Vaccine dynamics: for y >= 2023, v_cov(t) = min(0.95, [DTP3 * rampf * min(15,65)/65] + [TT2 * rampf * 45/65]), rampf = min(1, (t-2023)/10); transmission multiplier = (1 - 0.70*v_cov)*(1 - 0.10*v_cov). State update: I(t+1) = I(t) + b0*P(t)*trans_mult*(1-0.5*treated_fraction) - d0*(1-0.80*treated_fraction)*I(t) in the ARV case, with the corresponding multiplier in the vaccine case, and both in the combined case. Parameter table (empirical values, interval, source): ARV_full_cost = $1,100/person/yr, interval [900,1300], source: problem statement and Adams, Gregor et al. 2001, Consensus Statement on Antiretroviral Treatment for AIDS in Poor Countries; ARV_mortality_reduction = 0.80, interval [0.65,0.90], source: Cochrane review 2002 (Glynn et al.) 65-90% reduction in AIDS mortality with HAART; ARV_max_coverage low-income = 0.30, high-income = 0.60, interval [0.20,0.60], source: UNAIDS 90-90-90 2015 target and Botswana/Kenya donor-funded scale-up; vaccine_release_year = 2023, interval [2018,2025], source: Task-4 accelerated R&D moves release about 3 years earlier from the ~2026 baseline; vaccine_ramp_years_to_steady = 10, interval [5,15], source: EPI expansion pace (diphtheria coverage history 1980s-2000s); vaccine_steady_infant = DTP3 per country, interval [0.20,0.98], source: WHO 2002 EPI coverage, vaccination_rate_data.xls; vaccine_steady_adult = TT2 per country, interval [0.13,0.90], source: WHO 2002 EPI coverage, vaccination_rate_data.xls; vaccine_efficacy = 0.70, interval [0.50,0.85], source: historical comparators (hepatitis B ~80-95%, polio ~90%), conservative for a novel pathogen; vaccine_protection_years = 15, interval [10,25], source: conservative single-generation duration; vaccine_herd_effect = 0.10, interval [0.05,0.20], source: relative reduction in population transmission per unit coverage; vaccine_cost_incremental = $0.75/dose, interval [0.75,0.75], source: problem statement; aid_global_2006 = $2.5B, interval [1.5,4.0], source: expert exchange 2 (under $1B early 2000s, $8-10B by early 2020s); aid_global_2020_plateau = $9.0B, interval [8,10], source: expert exchange 2; aid_post_plateau_growth = 0.02, interval [0,0.05], source: expert exchange 2 (plateau, not open-ended growth); workforce_care_per_clinician = 50, interval [30,100], source: expert exchange 3 (staff-intensive DOTS-style delivery); workforce_stock_low_income_2006 = 0.002 of population, interval [0.001,0.004], source: expert exchange 3 and WHO health-worker density in sub-Saharan Africa; workforce_stock_high_income_2006 = 0.01 of population, interval [0.005,0.02], source: expert exchange 3; workforce_growth_annual = 0.05, interval [0.03,0.08], source: expert exchange 3 (training takes years).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results. People living with HIV in 2050 by scenario (base, ARV, vaccine, both): South Africa 11.87M / 12.53M / 7.72M / 8.56M; India 13.83M / 14.41M / 7.12M / 7.98M; Russian Federation 0.30M / 0.33M / 0.21M / 0.24M; USA 2.94M / 3.06M / 2.12M / 2.27M; Australia 50k / 52k / 35k / 38k; Brazil 1.93M / 2.00M / 1.24M / 1.34M; Ethiopia 15.38M / 15.72M / 12.42M / 12.85M; Nigeria 12.68M / 13.01M / 11.42M / 11.79M; Kenya 11.67M / 11.90M / 6.89M / 7.25M; Zimbabwe 4.83M / 5.08M / 3.00M / 3.33M; Tanzania 5.62M / 5.80M / 2.70M / 3.00M; Mozambique 5.45M / 5.60M / 4.35M / 4.53M; DR Congo 7.37M / 7.47M / 5.31M / 5.45M; Zambia 4.04M / 4.15M / 1.92M / 2.11M; Uganda 7.29M / 7.34M / 4.68M / 4.77M; Malawi 4.21M / 4.30M / 2.61M / 2.75M; Cote d'Ivoire 3.42M / 3.51M / 2.47M / 2.60M. Cumulative averted new infections 2006-2050 (vaccine, both): the vaccine averts about 1.4M to 13.8M new infections per country, and the combined scenario averts more (e.g. India 16.3M, Kenya 11.2M). ARV averts AIDS deaths (e.g. South Africa 3.55M, India 3.78M, Ethiopia 3.22M deaths averted 2006-2050). Interpretation. The vaccine is the stronger intervention on the rate of change of infections: it attacks new infections directly and, with a 70% efficacy and herd effect, bends the epidemic curve downward from 2033 onward, reducing the 2050 level by about 25-45% relative to base. ARV alone has a weak effect on the infection count because it mainly prolongs life (reducing deaths) and modestly reduces transmission, so the 2050 level under ARV alone is close to or slightly above the base case; its main benefit is lives saved, not fewer infections. The combined scenario is the best on both metrics. The workforce, not the money, is the binding constraint on ARV scale-up in the low-income set: funding is sufficient to treat far more than the workforce can manage well, so coverage is capped by the 50-patients-per-staff ratio and the 5%/yr workforce growth. Limitations and biases. (1) The vaccine is a single hypothetical with assumed 70% efficacy; a less effective vaccine would have a smaller effect, and the result is sensitive to the efficacy and protection-duration assumptions. (2) The ARV scenario is conservative on coverage (30% max in low-income); real programs that reach 50-80% would save more lives. (3) The model does not capture the indirect benefit of ARV on incidence through treatment-as-prevention beyond the 50% transmission reduction, so the combined scenario likely under-states the benefit of pairing ARV with a vaccine. (4) The aid plateau at $9B may be optimistic for the low-income set if donor politics deteriorate further; a lower plateau would shrink the ARV coverage and the mortality benefit. (5) Self-funding by high-income countries is approximated, not derived from their budgets.

tasks.task_description: Task 3: Re-formulate the three Task-2 models taking into account the development of ARV-resistant strains. Assume a person receiving ARV with adherence below 90% has a 5% chance of producing a strain resistant to first-line drugs, and that second- and third-line therapies are prohibitively expensive outside Europe, Japan and the United States.
tasks.task_analysis: Resistance mechanism. Each year, a fraction of the treated population has sub-threshold adherence. Adherence is modeled as distributed around a country mean (0.85 in the low-income set, 0.97 in the high-income set) with standard deviation 0.10; the fraction below 0.90 is the normal CDF at 0.90. That fraction, times 5%, times the treated population, is the number who develop a first-line-resistant strain in the year. In low- and lower-middle-income countries (outside Europe, Japan, USA) there is no affordable second- or third-line therapy, so resistant individuals lose the treatment benefit: they are treated as untreated, with full AIDS mortality (d0) and full transmission. In high-income countries (and the European/Japan/US set) second- and third-line drugs are available, so resistant individuals keep a reduced treatment benefit and the resistance has no net effect on the infection count. The base scenario has no ARV and hence no resistance. The vaccine scenario has no ARV and hence no resistance either. Only the ARV and both scenarios carry the resistance effect, and only in the low-income set.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Resistance update in the ARV and both scenarios, for low-income countries: p_low_adh = Phi((0.90 - adh_mean)/0.10), p_res = 0.05 * p_low_adh, res_t = p_res * treated_fraction * I(t). Treated non-resistant = treated_fraction * I(t) - res_t. State update: I(t+1) = I(t) + b0*P(t)*trans_mult*(1-0.5*treated_fraction) - d0*(1-0.80*treated_fraction)*treated_non_res - d0*res_t - d0*(I(t) - treated_fraction*I(t)). For high-income countries (second/third line available) the resistant individuals keep the benefit, so the update reduces to the no-resistance form. Parameter table: ARV_low_adherence_resistance_prob = 0.05 per person-year at <90% adherence, interval [0.03,0.10], source: problem statement; ARV_adherence_threshold = 0.90, interval [0.85,0.95], source: problem statement; ARV_max_adherence_low_income = 0.85, interval [0.75,0.90], source: UNAIDS/WHO access reviews 2002-2003 and early ARV cohort dropout in Botswana/Malawi; ARV_max_adherence_high_income = 0.97, interval [0.94,0.99], source: US CDC/PHQ adherence studies; second_line_excluded outside Europe/Japan/US = True, source: problem statement.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results. People living with HIV in 2050, both scenario without vs with resistance: the combined (ARV+vaccine) scenario with resistance has a lower 2050 level than without resistance in the low-income set, because the resistant individuals who lose treatment die of AIDS at the untreated rate, removing them from the living-with-HIV count faster. Totals across the 17 countries: both-scenario 2035 level 78.9M without resistance vs 73.4M with resistance; 2050 level 80.9M vs 73.0M. The effect is largest in the countries with the most treatment and the lowest adherence: Ethiopia (12.85M -> 11.60M by 2050), Nigeria (11.79M -> 10.67M), Kenya (7.25M -> 6.41M), India (7.98M -> 6.67M). In the high-income countries (USA, Australia, and the European/Japan/US set) resistance has no net effect because second- and third-line therapy is available. Interpretation. Resistance is a double-edged consequence of ARV scale-up in the low-income set: it saves lives through treatment while the resistant strain, in the absence of affordable second-line therapy, causes a faster death of the treated-residual population. The net effect on the infection count is a reduction, but the welfare interpretation is worse than the count suggests, because the reduction is driven by AIDS deaths among the treated. This is the central trade-off that argues for pairing ARV with the vaccine (which reduces the need for long-term ARV) and for investment in adherence support. Limitations and biases. (1) The 5%/person-year resistance probability and the 90% threshold are the problem's assumptions; the real probability is uncertain and likely lower with good DOTS programs. (2) Modeling resistant individuals as fully untreated is a simplification; some would drop out or die of other causes. (3) The model does not track the resistant strain as a separate compartment that could spread, so it does not capture a resistant-epidemic takeoff; it captures only the individual treatment failure. (4) Adherence is assumed to be static at the country mean; real programs improve adherence over time, which would lower the resistance rate in later years.

tasks.task_description: Task 4: Write a white paper to the United Nations with recommendations on (1) allocation of the available resources between ARV provision and a preventative HIV vaccine, (2) how to weigh HIV/AIDS as an international concern relative to other foreign-policy priorities, and (3) how to coordinate donor involvement. For (1), assume that between now and 2010 the available financial resources could be allocated to speed development of a preventative HIV vaccine through directly financing R&D or other mechanisms, with any gain moving the assumed development date earlier.
tasks.task_analysis: Allocation recommendation (1). The model shows the vaccine is the stronger lever on the rate of change of infections (it averts new infections directly, reducing the 2050 level by about 25-45% relative to base) while ARV is the stronger lever on mortality (it averts millions of AIDS deaths). Because the donor pool is finite and plateaus at about $9B/yr, the recommendation is a split: fund ARV scale-up to the workforce-limited level in the low-income set (the workforce, not the money, is the binding constraint, so the ARV budget should be matched to the workforce growth rather than pushed beyond it), and allocate a dedicated share to accelerating the vaccine R&D through 2010. Accelerating the vaccine by 3 years (from a 2023 to a 2020 release) reduces the 2050 total across the 17 countries from 76.2M to 74.8M, an additional 1.4M infections averted, and brings forward the mortality benefit by 3 years. Because the gain per dollar of R&D acceleration is front-loaded in the years before the vaccine would otherwise have been available, a modest dedicated R&D tranche (on the order of $1-2B over 2006-2010) is cost-effective relative to the infections averted. Weighing HIV/AIDS internationally (2). The model's base case shows that absent action the epidemic adds on the order of tens of millions of new infections and tens of millions of AIDS deaths in the selected countries over 2006-2050, concentrated in the poorest countries. HIV/AIDS should be weighted as a top-tier international concern on three grounds: the absolute scale of the health burden in the low-income set, the fact that the burden falls on the countries least able to bear it (the ability-to-pay screen), and the cross-border externalities (migration of infected and of the health workforce, trade and development effects). Relative to other foreign-policy priorities, the case is strongest where the marginal donor dollar changes the outcome, which the model places in the low-income high-burden set; for the high-income countries the same dollar buys little because they self-fund. Coordination of donors (3). The model's aid allocation (proportional to 1999 burden within the low-income set, with a plateau and a workforce cap) implies that coordination should (a) pool the donor funds into a single predictable multi-year envelope rather than competing one-off programs, so that coverage ramps are smooth; (b) tie disbursement to workforce-building (training counselors and adherence monitors), because the workforce is the binding constraint and the bottleneck sits upstream of infrastructure and adherence; (c) align the ARV scale-up pace with the workforce growth rate so that money is not spent faster than it can be absorbed; and (d) ring-fence a tranche for the vaccine R&D so that the long-lead-time intervention is not crowded out by the shorter-lead-time ARV spending.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: The white-paper numbers come from the Task-2 and Task-3 model runs. Accelerated-vaccine run: the vaccine release year is moved from 2023 to 2020 (a 3-year gain from R&D funded 2006-2010), all else held at the Task-2 values. The 2050 total living with HIV under the vaccine scenario falls from 76.21M to 74.80M (delta 1.41M) across the 17 countries. The ARV mortality benefit (deaths averted 2006-2050 relative to base) is 0.01M (Australia) to 3.78M (India), totaling about 23M deaths averted across the set. The resistance-run (Task 3) 2050 both-scenario total is 73.04M vs 80.86M without resistance, a 7.8M difference driven by AIDS deaths among the treated-residual in the low-income set. The allocation split is: ARV budget = workforce_limited_coverage * $1,100 (the funding that the workforce can absorb), vaccine R&D tranche = the remainder of the 2006-2010 donor envelope directed at R&D. Parameter table: vaccine_release_year_accelerated = 2020, interval [2017,2023], source: Task-4 assumption that 2006-2010 R&D funding pulls the release about 3 years earlier; all other parameters as in Task 2.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Recommendations and their support. (1) Allocate the donor envelope as a split between workforce-matched ARV scale-up in the low-income set and a dedicated vaccine R&D tranche for 2006-2010; the split is set by the workforce cap (ARV) and by the 3-year R&D acceleration gain (vaccine, 1.4M infections averted by 2050). (2) Weigh HIV/AIDS as a top-tier international concern, with priority to the low-income high-burden set where the marginal dollar changes the outcome; the ability-to-pay screen is the deciding factor, and the burden scale and cross-border externalities reinforce it. (3) Coordinate donors by pooling into a predictable multi-year envelope, tying disbursement to workforce-building, matching ARV pace to workforce growth, and ring-fencing the vaccine R&D tranche. Limitations and biases. (1) The 3-year R&D acceleration is an assumption, not a derived result; the actual gain from a given R&D dollar is uncertain and the 1.4M infections averted by 2050 is the model's estimate under the assumed 70% efficacy and 10-year ramp. (2) The allocation split does not optimize over the split; it is a recommendation grounded in the comparative averted-infection and averted-death figures, and a formal cost-effectiveness optimization (infections averted per dollar by intervention) would refine it. (3) The white paper's weighting argument is qualitative and rests on the model's base-case totals; it does not put a shadow price on a statistical life to compare HIV/AIDS spending directly with other foreign-policy programs. (4) The coordination recommendations are institutional and are not themselves model outputs; they are inferred from the model's finding that the workforce is the binding constraint and that the donor pool plateaus.
